30: ## 2. OVERVIEW
31: 
32: ### Why This Skill Exists
33: 
34: Driving a browser from an agent usually means a heavyweight automation framework or burning tokens on verbose protocol dumps. A one-shot screenshot or a console read wants a fast single-purpose command. A multi-step flow that chains browser actions with other tool calls wants a typed composable interface. Picking the wrong approach wastes tokens or blocks parallelism. A single tool does not fit both needs, so this skill gives you two paths and routes between them.
35: 
36: ### What It Does
37: 
38: This skill drives a real browser through two complementary paths. The `bdg` CLI is fast and token-efficient. It is self-documenting at every level and reaches the full Chrome DevTools Protocol surface. The Code Mode MCP path runs isolated browser instances for parallel sessions and multi-tool chaining. A routing rule picks the right path for the work at hand, so a quick screenshot never pays the MCP overhead and a complex chain never blocks on a single session.
39: 
40: The MCP transport is owned by `mcp-code-mode`. This skill consumes Code Mode as a provider and does not implement the transport. For generated application code that gets inspected, `sk-code` owns the standards and tests.

100: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
101: 
102: ### The Routing Rule
103: 
104: The skill prefers the CLI for fast low-token inspection. It switches to the MCP path when browser work must chain with other tools or run as parallel isolated sessions. A weighted intent scorer reads the request text for keywords such as "bdg" or "screenshot", plus phrases like "parallel sessions". It then loads only the reference files relevant to the chosen path.
105: 
106: ### The CLI Path
107: 
108: `bdg` starts a Chrome session and sends CDP commands over WebSocket. Artifacts land on disk. It is self-documenting at every level. `bdg cdp --list` lists every CDP domain. `bdg cdp --describe Page` enumerates the methods in a domain with their signatures. `bdg cdp --search screenshot` finds every CDP method whose name or description contains the term. Because the CLI reaches the full protocol surface, you can compose arbitrary CDP workflows and pipe results through Unix tools.
109: 
110: ```bash
111: bdg cdp --list | head -5
112: # Page
113: # DOM
114: # Network
115: # Runtime
116: # Emulation
117: 
118: bdg cdp --describe Page | head -3
119: # Page.enable
120: # Page.disable
121: # Page.navigate
122: ```
123: 
124: ### The MCP Path
125: 
126: The MCP path registers `chrome-devtools-mcp@0.26.0` entries with `--isolated=true`. Each entry runs its own browser process, so parallel sessions and multi-tool chaining do not interfere. Tool naming follows the Code Mode convention: `{manual_name}.{manual_name}_{tool_name}`. Tools return data as objects inside a `call_tool_chain()` block instead of writing files to disk. Always close pages in a `finally` block so cleanup runs even on errors.

130: | Navigation | `navigate_page` |
131: | Screenshots | `take_screenshot` |
132: | Viewport control | `resize_page` |
133: | Interaction | `click`, `fill`, `hover`, `press_key` |
134: | Session control | `new_page`, `select_page`, `close_page` |
135: 
136: The CLI path covers the same actions and reaches the full CDP surface beyond the curated set.

140: `--isolated=true` is the key to parallelism. Register several entries in `.utcp_config.json`, each with its own name such as `chrome_devtools_1` and `chrome_devtools_2`. Each entry gets its own browser process. Inside a single `call_tool_chain()` block you can navigate two isolated browsers and capture both screenshots. The results return together, with no session conflicts and no port collisions.

12: 
13: # mcp-chrome-devtools
14: 
15: > Drive a real browser from your agent or terminal: a fast CLI for one-shot inspection and an MCP path for parallel isolated sessions.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
20: 
21: | Aspect | What you get |
22: |---|---|
23: | **Use it for** | Browser screenshots, console inspection, network traces and CDP automation from an agent or terminal |
24: | **Invoke with** | "chrome devtools", "browser debugging", "bdg", "screenshot" or auto-routing on browser keywords |
25: | **Works on** | Chrome, Chromium and Edge through a local browser instance |
26: | **Produces** | PNG screenshots, HAR network traces, console logs, DOM query results and CDP responses |
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 2. OVERVIEW
31: 
32: ### Why This Skill Exists
33: 
34: Driving a browser from an agent usually means a heavyweight automation framework or burning tokens on verbose protocol dumps. A one-shot screenshot or a console read wants a fast single-purpose command. A multi-step flow that chains browser actions with other tool calls wants a typed composable interface. Picking the wrong approach wastes tokens or blocks parallelism. A single tool does not fit both needs, so this skill gives you two paths and routes between them.
35: 
36: ### What It Does
37: 
38: This skill drives a real browser through two complementary paths. The `bdg` CLI is fast and token-efficient. It is self-documenting at every level and reaches the full Chrome DevTools Protocol surface. The Code Mode MCP path runs isolated browser instances for parallel sessions and multi-tool chaining. A routing rule picks the right path for the work at hand, so a quick screenshot never pays the MCP overhead and a complex chain never blocks on a single session.
39: 
40: The MCP transport is owned by `mcp-code-mode`. This skill consumes Code Mode as a provider and does not implement the transport. For generated application code that gets inspected, `sk-code` owns the standards and tests.
41: 
42: ### The CDP Capability Surface
43: 
44: | Capability | What the skill can operate |
45: |---|---|
46: | **Screenshots** | capture page and element screenshots as PNG files |
47: | **Console and network** | read console messages, runtime errors and HAR network traces |
48: | **DOM** | query, inspect and drive page elements at the protocol level |
49: | **Protocol reach** | discover and call any Chrome DevTools Protocol domain through the `bdg cdp` surface |
50: | **Parallel sessions** | run isolated browser instances side by side through Code Mode |
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## 3. QUICK START
55: 
56: **Step 1: Install the CLI.**
57: 
58: ```bash
59: npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha
60: ```
61: 
62: Confirm the binary and its version:
63: 
64: ```bash
65: command -v bdg
66: # Expected: /usr/local/bin/bdg or a similar PATH entry
67: 
68: bdg --version
69: # Expected: browser-debugger-cli@x.x.x
70: ```
71: 
72: **Step 2: Capture a screenshot.**
73: 
74: ```bash
75: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
76: bdg dom screenshot /tmp/example.png 2>&1
77: bdg stop 2>&1
78: ls -la /tmp/example.png
79: ```
80: 
81: The last command lists the file, which must exist as a valid PNG. `bdg stop` ends the session so no browser process lingers.
82: 
83: **Step 3: Use the MCP path with Code Mode.**
84: 
85: The `chrome_devtools_1` and `chrome_devtools_2` manuals in `.utcp_config.json` pin `chrome-devtools-mcp@0.26.0` with `--isolated=true`. Run browser operations inside a `call_tool_chain()` block:
86: 
87: ```typescript
88: call_tool_chain(`
89:   await chrome_devtools_1.chrome_devtools_1_navigate_page({ url: "https://example.com" })
90:   const screenshot = await chrome_devtools_1.chrome_devtools_1_take_screenshot({})
91:   const logs = await chrome_devtools_1.chrome_devtools_1_list_console_messages({})
92:   return { screenshot, logs }
93: `)
94: ```
95: 
96: The block returns a screenshot and console messages as typed objects.
97: 
98: ---
99: 
100: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
101: 
102: ### The Routing Rule
103: 
104: The skill prefers the CLI for fast low-token inspection. It switches to the MCP path when browser work must chain with other tools or run as parallel isolated sessions. A weighted intent scorer reads the request text for keywords such as "bdg" or "screenshot", plus phrases like "parallel sessions". It then loads only the reference files relevant to the chosen path.
105: 
106: ### The CLI Path
107: 
108: `bdg` starts a Chrome session and sends CDP commands over WebSocket. Artifacts land on disk. It is self-documenting at every level. `bdg cdp --list` lists every CDP domain. `bdg cdp --describe Page` enumerates the methods in a domain with their signatures. `bdg cdp --search screenshot` finds every CDP method whose name or description contains the term. Because the CLI reaches the full protocol surface, you can compose arbitrary CDP workflows and pipe results through Unix tools.
109: 
110: ```bash
111: bdg cdp --list | head -5
112: # Page
113: # DOM
114: # Network
115: # Runtime
116: # Emulation
117: 
118: bdg cdp --describe Page | head -3
119: # Page.enable
120: # Page.disable
121: # Page.navigate
122: ```
123: 
124: ### The MCP Path
125: 
126: The MCP path registers `chrome-devtools-mcp@0.26.0` entries with `--isolated=true`. Each entry runs its own browser process, so parallel sessions and multi-tool chaining do not interfere. Tool naming follows the Code Mode convention: `{manual_name}.{manual_name}_{tool_name}`. Tools return data as objects inside a `call_tool_chain()` block instead of writing files to disk. Always close pages in a `finally` block so cleanup runs even on errors.
127: 
128: | Need | Tool |
129: |---|---|
130: | Navigation | `navigate_page` |
131: | Screenshots | `take_screenshot` |
132: | Viewport control | `resize_page` |
133: | Interaction | `click`, `fill`, `hover`, `press_key` |
134: | Session control | `new_page`, `select_page`, `close_page` |
135: 
136: The CLI path covers the same actions and reaches the full CDP surface beyond the curated set.
137: 
138: ### Isolated Instances
139: 
140: `--isolated=true` is the key to parallelism. Register several entries in `.utcp_config.json`, each with its own name such as `chrome_devtools_1` and `chrome_devtools_2`. Each entry gets its own browser process. Inside a single `call_tool_chain()` block you can navigate two isolated browsers and capture both screenshots. The results return together, with no session conflicts and no port collisions.
141: 
142: ### Example Workflows
143: 
144: The skill ships three production scripts under `examples/`. Each doubles as an end-to-end workflow and a CI-ready test.
145: 
146: - `performance-baseline.sh [URL] [OUTPUT_DIR]` captures metrics, a HAR trace, a screenshot, console logs and DOM stats into timestamped files. The output lands in a `performance-baselines/` directory with JSON for metrics and console logs, a HAR file for the network trace and a PNG for the visual baseline.
147: - `animation-testing.sh` asserts layout count, recalculation count and task-duration thresholds, captures before and after screenshots and exits non-zero on any failure. It targets a selector and an animation trigger class so you can test any animated element on the page.
148: - `multi-viewport-test.sh` runs five viewports (desktop 1920x1080, laptop 1366x768, tablet 768x1024, mobile 375x667, mobile-large 414x896) and fails on any console error. It captures an initial and an animated screenshot per viewport and writes a per-viewport summary.
149: 
150: All three scripts under `examples/` support headless mode through `CHROME_HEADLESS=true` and return semantic exit codes. They fit straight into CI pipelines.
151: 
152: ---
153: 
154: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
155: 
156: ### When To Use This Skill
157: 
158: - Reach for this skill when you need a browser screenshot, a console read, a network trace or a CDP operation from an agent.
159: - Reach for the CLI when the work is a single inspection.
160: - Reach for the MCP path when you are already using Code Mode for other tools or need parallel isolated browsers.
161: - Reach for the example scripts when you want a pre-built CI workflow.
162: 
163: This skill is not a cross-browser test framework. The CLI targets Chromium-based browsers only:
164: 
165: - Supported: Chrome, Chromium and Edge
166: - Not covered: Firefox and Safari. Cross-browser suites such as Puppeteer, Playwright or Selenium need a dedicated framework
167: 
168: ### Related Skills
169: 
170: | Skill | Relationship |
171: |---|---|
172: | `mcp-code-mode` | Owns the MCP transport. This skill registers Chrome DevTools as a Code Mode provider and calls tools through `call_tool_chain()`. |
173: | `sk-code` | Owns application-code standards and tests. This skill verifies browser behavior that `sk-code` produces. |
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
178: 
179: | What you see | Why | Fix |
180: |---|---|---|
181: | `command not found: bdg` | CLI not installed or npm global bin not on PATH | `npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha` and verify PATH with `npm config get prefix` |
182: | `Could not find Chrome` | Chrome path not set or binary missing | Set `CHROME_PATH` to the browser executable and confirm with `ls -la "$CHROME_PATH"` |
183: | `Another session already active` | A prior session was not stopped | Run `bdg stop`. In scripts, register `trap "bdg stop" EXIT INT TERM` |
184: | `Method not found` | A guessed CDP method name | Use `bdg cdp --search <term>` to find the real name, never hardcode method names |
185: | `jq` parse error | stderr is contaminating stdout | Append `2>&1` before piping to `jq` |
186: | MCP tools missing | The `.utcp_config.json` entry is missing or disabled | Confirm the entry exists with `disabled: false` and restart the session |
187: 
188: ---
189: 
190: ## 7. FAQ
191: 
192: **Q: When do I use the CLI versus the MCP path?**
193: 
194: A: Use the CLI for a one-shot screenshot or a console read where speed and low token cost matter. The CLI also covers network traces. Use the MCP path when you need to chain browser operations with other MCP tools or run parallel isolated browsers. If the CLI is available and no chaining is needed, the CLI wins.
195: 
196: **Q: How do I prevent browser processes from piling up?**
197: 
198: A: Run `bdg stop` after each session. In scripts, register `trap "bdg stop" EXIT INT TERM` so cleanup runs even on failure. For MCP sessions, wrap browser calls in `try/finally` and close pages in the `finally` block.
199: 
200: **Q: Can I use this with Firefox or Safari?**
201: 
202: A: No. The CLI targets Chromium-based browsers only. For other engines, reach for a dedicated framework such as Puppeteer or Playwright. See INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION for the full boundary.
203: 
204: **Q: How do I keep CDP method names stable across Chrome versions?**
205: 
206: A: Do not hardcode method names. Discover the current names with the `bdg cdp` commands before running them. `bdg cdp --list` shows every domain. `bdg cdp --describe <domain>` lists the methods in a domain. `bdg cdp --search <term>` finds methods by name or description. The discovery commands always reflect the connected Chrome version.
207: 
208: **Q: How do I configure parallel isolated MCP instances?**
209: 
210: A: Register multiple entries in `.utcp_config.json`, each with its own name such as `chrome_devtools_1` and `chrome_devtools_2`, with `--isolated=true` on every entry. Each entry gets its own browser process. Use them in parallel inside the same `call_tool_chain()` block.
211: 
212: ---
213:

215:

219: |---|---|
220: | README structure | `python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/scripts/validate_document.py .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-chrome-devtools/README.md --type readme` reports zero issues |

223: | MCP health | Confirm `chrome_devtools` tools appear in `list_tools()` output and a `navigate_page` call completes without connection errors |
224: | Example scripts | Run `performance-baseline.sh`, `animation-testing.sh` and `multi-viewport-test.sh` in headless mode and confirm all exit zero |
225:

20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |

33:

35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.

47:

53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |

55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64:

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---

14: # Chrome DevTools Orchestrator - CLI + MCP Integration Router
15: 
16: The machine router for [`SKILL.md`](./SKILL.md). `SKILL.md` keeps the short routing prose and the
17: link that points here; this file holds the declaration a reader parses to decide what loads.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Requests reach this skill when they name browser debugging, Chrome DevTools, CDP, `bdg` or `browser-debugger-cli`, when they ask for a screenshot, HAR export, console log, network inspection, DOM query or an in-browser script, when they need a CI-ready automation script, or when a Chrome DevTools MCP call chains browser work with other tools or runs parallel isolated sessions. It routes to three resource families: `references/cdp-patterns.md` for the CDP command patterns, `references/session-management.md` for the session lifecycle, and `references/troubleshooting.md` for an install, a failure, or the fuller diagnostics an on-demand keyword requests.
24: 
25: The router answers one question: given a request, which skill-local resources load, in what order, and
26: what happens when nothing matches. Every path below stays inside this skill folder, and no resource
27: loads before an intent selects it.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. INTENT MODEL
32: 
33: - **`CLI`** (weight 4) fires on "bdg", "browser-debugger-cli", "terminal", "cli", "command line", "shell", "headless", "lightweight" and "token efficient", and a `bdg` binary on PATH adds 5 on top. It loads `references/cdp-patterns.md` and `references/session-management.md`.
34: - **`MCP`** (weight 4) fires on "mcp", "code mode", "multi-tool", "tool chain", "isolated instances", "parallel sessions" and "in parallel", and a configured Code Mode adds 4 on top. It loads `references/session-management.md` and `references/cdp-patterns.md`.
35: - **`INSTALL`** (weight 4) fires on "install", "setup", "not installed", "not found", "command -v bdg", "npm install", "getting started" and "first time". It loads `references/troubleshooting.md`.
36: - **`TROUBLESHOOT`** (weight 4) fires on "error", "failed", "troubleshoot", "keeps dropping", "won't connect", "hangs", "stuck", "not working" and "root cause", and a request carrying an error adds 4 on top. It loads `references/troubleshooting.md`.
37: - **`AUTOMATION`** (weight 3) fires on "ci", "continuous integration", "pipeline", "automation", "production", "automate" and "batch". It loads `references/cdp-patterns.md` and `references/session-management.md`.
38: 
39: The two highest-scoring intents load together when their scores sit within 1.0 of each other, at most two intents per request, and a request that scores on none loads nothing: it returns `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST`, and `references/cdp-patterns.md` is suggested beside that checklist as a fallback-only default, so it never enters a scored route's loaded set. A scoring `ON_DEMAND_KEYWORDS` term then adds `references/troubleshooting.md` and `references/session-management.md` on top of the scored set.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 3. MACHINE ROUTER
44: 
45: The one machine-readable projection of the intent model above, written as `## MACHINE ROUTER` so every
46: reader finds it. This section is the last in the file, and it holds the only pseudocode.
47: 
48: The routing detail behind the summary above: the loading levels, the resilience bullets and the router pseudocode that reads them.
49: 
50: ### Resource Loading Levels
51: 
52: | Level       | When to Load             | Resources                       |
53: | ----------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
54: | CONDITIONAL | If intent signals match  | CLI/MCP/session/troubleshooting |
55: | ON_DEMAND   | Only on explicit request | Full diagnostics set            |
56: | FALLBACK    | Zero-score routes only   | Core CDP pattern reference suggested (never auto-loaded) |
57: 
58: ### Smart Router Pseudocode
59: 
60: The authoritative routing logic for scoped loading, weighted intent scoring, and ambiguity handling.
61: 
62: The shared helper bodies are documented once in [`shared-smart-router.md`](../../system-spec-kit/references/cli/shared-smart-router.md).
63: 
64: - Pattern 1: Simple Intent Routing - CLI/MCP/install/troubleshoot/automation intents select the real flat `references/*.md` resources. This skill currently has no keyed `references/<key>/` or `assets/<key>/` resource subdirectories.
65: - Pattern 2: Multi-Tier Graceful Fallback - `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` requests CLI/MCP/session disambiguation and SUGGESTS the default CDP reference without loading it (`DEFAULT_RESOURCE_SEMANTICS = "fallback-only"`): a scored route loads exactly its intents' mapped resources, and a zero-score route loads nothing beyond the disambiguation checklist.
66: 
67: ```python
68: from pathlib import Path
69: 
70: SKILL_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
71: RESOURCE_BASES = (SKILL_ROOT / "references", SKILL_ROOT / "assets")
72: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/cdp-patterns.md"
73: # Fallback-only: DEFAULT_RESOURCE is a defer-time suggestion, never unioned
74: # into a route's loaded set. Scored routes load exactly RESOURCE_MAP[intent];
75: # zero-score routes load nothing and ask for disambiguation instead.
76: DEFAULT_RESOURCE_SEMANTICS = "fallback-only"
77: 
78: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = [
79:     "Confirm CLI vs MCP path",
80:     "Confirm target browser/session",
81:     "Provide one error, URL, or task goal",
82: ]
83: 
84: INTENT_SIGNALS = {
85:     "CLI": {"weight": 4, "keywords": ["bdg", "browser-debugger-cli", "terminal", "cli", "command line", "command-line", "shell", "headless", "lightweight", "token efficient"]},
86:     "MCP": {"weight": 4, "keywords": ["mcp", "code mode", "multi-tool", "parallel sessions", "model context protocol", "multiple tools", "isolated instances", "tool chain", "in parallel"]},
87:     "INSTALL": {"weight": 4, "keywords": ["install", "setup", "not installed", "command -v bdg", "set up", "getting started", "download", "npm install", "not found", "first time"]},
88:     "TROUBLESHOOT": {"weight": 4, "keywords": ["error", "failed", "troubleshoot", "session issue", "keeps dropping", "won't connect", "figure out why", "work out the cause", "hangs", "hanging", "stuck", "crash", "crashing", "broken", "not working", "timeout", "disconnect", "flaky", "root cause"]},
89:     "AUTOMATION": {"weight": 3, "keywords": ["ci", "pipeline", "automation", "production", "automate", "unattended", "continuous integration", "batch", "recurring"]},
90: }
91: 
92: RESOURCE_MAP = {
93:     "CLI": ["references/cdp-patterns.md", "references/session-management.md"],
94:     "MCP": ["references/session-management.md", "references/cdp-patterns.md"],
95:     "INSTALL": ["references/troubleshooting.md"],
96:     "TROUBLESHOOT": ["references/troubleshooting.md"],
97:     "AUTOMATION": ["references/cdp-patterns.md", "references/session-management.md"],
98: }
99: 
100: LOADING_LEVELS = {
101:     "ON_DEMAND_KEYWORDS": ["full troubleshooting", "full session guide", "all patterns", "capture a har", "console errors", "routing dashboard", "staging", "devtools"],
102:     "ON_DEMAND": ["references/troubleshooting.md", "references/session-management.md"],
103: }
104: 
105: def _task_text(task) -> str:
106:     parts = [
107:         str(getattr(task, "text", "")),
108:         str(getattr(task, "query", "")),
109:         " ".join(getattr(task, "keywords", []) or []),
110:     ]
111:     return " ".join(parts).lower()
112: 
113: def _guard_in_skill(relative_path: str) -> str:
114:     resolved = (SKILL_ROOT / relative_path).resolve()
115:     resolved.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT)
116:     if resolved.suffix.lower() != ".md":
117:         raise ValueError(f"Only markdown resources are routable: {relative_path}")
118:     return resolved.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT).as_posix()
119: 
120: def discover_markdown_resources() -> set[str]:
121:     docs = []
122:     for base in RESOURCE_BASES:
123:         if base.exists():
124:             docs.extend(p for p in base.rglob("*.md") if p.is_file())
125:     return {doc.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT).as_posix() for doc in docs}
126: 
127: def score_intents(task) -> dict[str, float]:
128:     """Weighted intent scoring from request text and routing signals."""
129:     text = _task_text(task)
130:     scores = {intent: 0.0 for intent in INTENT_SIGNALS}
131:     for intent, cfg in INTENT_SIGNALS.items():
132:         for keyword in cfg["keywords"]:
133:             if keyword in text:
134:                 scores[intent] += cfg["weight"]

51: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
52: 
53: ### Tool Comparison
54: 
55: Prefer CLI (`bdg`) for fast, low-token browser inspection. Use MCP via Code Mode when browser work must be chained with other tools or parallel isolated sessions.
56: 
57: ### CLI Approach (Priority) - browser-debugger-cli (bdg)
58: 
59: #### Installation & Verification
60: 
61: Check with `command -v bdg`, install with `npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha`, then verify `bdg --version 2>&1`.
62: 
63: ### MCP Approach (Fallback) - Chrome DevTools via Code Mode
64: 
65: When CLI unavailable or multi-tool integration needed.
66: 
67: #### Prerequisites
68: 
69: 1. Code Mode configured in `.utcp_config.json`
70: 2. Chrome DevTools MCP server registered with `--isolated=true`
71: 
72: #### Isolated Instances
73: 
74: **Key Feature**: MCP uses `--isolated=true` flag for independent browser instances.
75: 
76: **Benefits of isolated instances:**
77: - Each instance runs in its own browser process
78: - Multiple parallel browser sessions possible
79: - No session conflicts between instances
80: - Register multiple instances for parallel testing (e.g., `chrome_devtools_1`, `chrome_devtools_2`)
81: 
82: Configure one or more Chrome DevTools MCP entries in `.utcp_config.json` with `--isolated=true` when parallel browser sessions are needed.
83: 
84: #### Configuration Check
85: 
86: ```bash
87: cat .utcp_config.json | jq '.manual_call_templates[] | select(.name | startswith("chrome_devtools"))'
88: ```
89: 
90: #### Invocation Pattern
91: 
92: Tool naming is `{manual_name}.{manual_name}_{tool_name}`. Run MCP browser operations inside `call_tool_chain()` and close pages in a `finally` block.
93: 
94: #### Available MCP Tools
95: 
96: Common MCP tools include navigation, screenshots, console messages, viewport resize, clicks, form fill, hover, keyboard, waits, page creation/selection/close. Use underscores in tool names and confirm exact names with Code Mode discovery.
97: 
98: #### When to Prefer MCP
99: 
100: - Already using Code Mode for other tools (external services, Figma, etc.)
101: - Need to chain browser operations with other MCP tools
102: - **Parallel browser testing** - compare multiple sites/viewports simultaneously
103: - Complex multi-step automation in TypeScript
104: - Type-safe tool invocation required
105: 
106: #### MCP Limitations
107: 
108: - Higher token cost than CLI
109: - Requires Code Mode infrastructure
110: - Subset of CDP methods (CLI has 300+ methods across 53 domains)
111: - Less self-documenting than CLI's `--list`, `--describe`
112: 
113: ### MCP Session Cleanup
114: 
115: Always close browser instances when done. Wrap Code Mode browser operations in `try/finally` so cleanup runs even on errors.

556: done
557: 
558: # Batch cookie extraction
559: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
560: bdg network getCookies 2>&1 | jq -r '.[] | "\(.name)=\(.value)"' | \
561: while read cookie; do
562:   echo "$cookie" >> cookies.txt
563: done
564: bdg stop 2>&1
565: ```
566: 
567: ---
568: 
569: ### Pattern 5: Error Stream Separation
570: 
571: ```bash
572: # Capture stderr separately
573: bdg cdp Page.navigate '{"url":"invalid"}' 2>errors.log 1>output.json
574: 
575: # Check exit code
576: bdg status 2>&1
577: if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
578:   echo "Session check failed"
579:   cat errors.log
580: fi
581: 
582: # Discard stderr
583: bdg cdp Network.enable 2>/dev/null
584: 
585: # Combine and filter
586: (bdg console --list 2>&1 | jq '.') || echo "Command failed"
587: ```
588: 
589: ---
590: 
591: ## 7. DISCOVERY PATTERN EXAMPLES
592: 
593: ### Before/After: Progressive Disclosure
594: 
595: ❌ **BEFORE** (Anti-pattern - Guessing method names):
596: ```bash
597: # Guessing method names without discovery
598: bdg cdp Page.screenshot 2>&1  # FAILS - wrong method name
599: bdg cdp Screenshot 2>&1       # FAILS - wrong domain
600: bdg cdp capture 2>&1          # FAILS - incomplete name
601: 
602: # Results in: "Error: Method not found"
603: # Wastes time with trial and error
604: ```
605: 
606: ✅ **AFTER** (Correct - Progressive disclosure):
607: ```bash
608: # Step 1: List all domains
609: bdg cdp --list  # → Discover "Page" domain exists
610: 
611: **Validation**: `domains_discovered`
612: 
613: # Step 2: Explore specific domain
614: bdg cdp --describe Page  # → Find "captureScreenshot" method
615: 
616: **Validation**: `method_identified`
617: 
618: # Step 3: Get method details
619: bdg cdp --describe Page.captureScreenshot  # → See parameters and return type
620: 
621: **Validation**: `signature_understood`
622: 
623: # Step 4: Execute discovered method
624: bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1
625: 
626: **Validation**: `execution_successful`
627: ```
628: 
629: **Why better**: No guessing, documentation always current, clear understanding before execution, eliminates trial-and-error.
630: 
631: **Finding Methods by Use Case**:
632: 
633: ```bash
634: # Find cookie-related methods
635: bdg cdp --search cookie
636: 
637: # Find performance methods
638: bdg cdp --search performance
639: 
640: # Find DOM manipulation
641: bdg cdp --search DOM
642: 
643: # Find network interception
644: bdg cdp --search intercept
645: ```
646: 
647: ---
648: 
649: ## 8. ADVANCED PATTERNS
650: 
651: ### Sequential Sessions Only (bdg Has No Session Selector)
652: 
653: Live `bdg 0.6.10 --help` exposes one global `status` / `stop` lifecycle with no session-id, name, or selector option, so backgrounding two `bdg <url>` invocations does not give two independently addressable sessions: `bdg status` always reports the single active session, and killing a captured `$!` PID bypasses bdg's own cleanup instead of using it. Finish one session (start, use, `bdg stop`) before starting the next:
654: 
655: ```bash
656: # Session 1: start, use, stop
657: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
658: bdg status 2>&1
659: # ... run the CDP/dom/network/console commands for this session ...
660: bdg stop 2>&1
661: 
662: # Session 2: only after session 1 has been stopped
663: bdg https://test.com 2>&1
664: bdg status 2>&1
665: # ... run the CDP/dom/network/console commands for this session ...
666: bdg stop 2>&1
667: ```
668: 
669: For genuine parallel browser control, use `mcp-chrome-devtools`'s multiple registered MCP instances (`chrome_devtools_1`, `chrome_devtools_2` in `.utcp_config.json`, see `SKILL.md`) instead of backgrounding the `bdg` CLI.
670: 
671: ### Conditional Execution
672: 
673: ```bash
674: # Execute CDP only if session active
675: if bdg status 2>&1 | grep -q "active"; then
676:   bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1
677: else
678:   echo "No active session"
679: fi
680: 
681: # Retry with exponential backoff
682: for i in {1..5}; do
683:   bdg https://example.com 2>&1 && break
684:   echo "Retry $i failed, waiting..."
685:   sleep $((2**i))
686: done
687: ```
688: 
689: ### Data Extraction Pipelines
690: 
691: ```bash
692: # Extract, transform, load pattern
693: bdg https://example.com 2>&1 && \
694: bdg dom eval "document.querySelectorAll('a')" 2>&1 | \
695: jq -r '.result.value[] | .href' | \
696: sort -u > links.txt && \
697: bdg stop 2>&1
698: 
699: # Performance monitoring pipeline
700: bdg https://example.com 2>&1 && \
701: bdg cdp Performance.enable 2>&1 && \
702: sleep 5 && \
703: bdg cdp Performance.getMetrics 2>&1 | \
704: jq '.result.metrics[] | select(.name | contains("DOM"))' > perf.json && \
705: bdg stop 2>&1
706: ```
707: 
708: ---
709: 
710: ## 9. BEST PRACTICES
711: 
712: 1. **Always verify session status** before executing CDP commands
713: 2. **Use helpers when available** (simpler than raw CDP)
714: 3. **Capture stderr** with `2>&1` for comprehensive error handling
715: 4. **Use jq for JSON processing** instead of string manipulation
716: 5. **Clean up sessions** with `bdg stop` after completion
717: 6. **Progressive disclosure** - start with --describe before executing
718: 7. **Case-insensitive method names** - bdg normalizes automatically
719: 8. **Semantic exit codes** - check `$?` for scripting
720:

649: ## 8. ADVANCED PATTERNS

651: ### Sequential Sessions Only (bdg Has No Session Selector)
652: 
653: Live `bdg 0.6.10 --help` exposes one global `status` / `stop` lifecycle with no session-id, name, or selector option, so backgrounding two `bdg <url>` invocations does not give two independently addressable sessions: `bdg status` always reports the single active session, and killing a captured `$!` PID bypasses bdg's own cleanup instead of using it. 658: bdg status 2>&1

660: bdg stop 2>&1
661: 
662: # Session 2: only after session 1 has been stopped
663: bdg https://test.com 2>&1
664: bdg status 2>&1
665: # ... run the CDP/dom/network/console commands for this session ...
666: bdg stop 2>&1
667: ```

236: ## 6. MULTI-SESSION MANAGEMENT
237: 
238: ### Sequential Session Labeling (No True Concurrency)
239: 
240: Live `bdg 0.6.10 --help` exposes one global `status` / `stop` lifecycle with no session-id, name, or selector option. A locally-tracked bash label does not select a specific bdg session: every `bdg status` / `bdg stop` call still targets the single active session, so two "tracked" sessions started back to back are not actually isolated from each other, and the second `bdg <url>` replaces the first. Label sessions for reporting only, and fully finish one (start, verify, use, stop) before starting the next. For true parallel browser control, use the `mcp-tooling/mcp-chrome-devtools` MCP surface's multiple registered instances (see `SKILL.md`) instead of the `bdg` CLI.
241: 
242: ```bash
243: #!/bin/bash
244: # Label sessions for reporting, but process them one at a time.
245: # bdg has exactly one active session; there is no selector to address a
246: # specific labeled session once it is running.
247: 
248: # Session tracking (label -> url, for reporting only)
249: declare -A SESSIONS
250: 
251: run_labeled_session() {
252:   local name=$1
253:   local url=$2
254: 
255:   echo "Starting session: $name"
256:   bdg "$url" 2>&1
257:   SESSIONS[$name]="$url"
258: 
259:   if bdg status 2>&1 | grep -q "active"; then
260:     echo "✓ Session $name active"
261:   else
262:     echo "✗ Session $name failed"
263:     unset SESSIONS[$name]
264:     return 1
265:   fi
266: 
267:   # ... do the work for this session here, before it is stopped ...
268: 
269:   echo "Stopping session: $name"
270:   bdg stop 2>&1
271:   unset SESSIONS[$name]
272: }
273: 
274: # Usage: fully start, use, and stop one session before starting the next
275: run_labeled_session "production" "https://example.com"
276: run_labeled_session "staging" "https://staging.example.com"
277: ```

495: ## 9. SESSION CLEANUP
496: 
497: ### Before/After: Cleanup Patterns

499: ❌ **BEFORE** (Anti-pattern - No cleanup):

508: # Script exits without stopping session
509: # → Browser process remains running
510: # → Session resources not released
511: # → Next script may fail with "session already active"
512: ```

515: ```bash
516: #!/bin/bash

518: 
519: cleanup() {
520:   echo "Cleaning up session..."
521:   bdg stop 2>&1 > /dev/null
522:   echo "✓ Cleanup complete"
523: }
524: 
525: # Register cleanup on EXIT, INT (Ctrl+C), TERM
526: trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM
527: 
528: **Validation**: `cleanup_registered`
529: 
530: # Session work
531: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
532: bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
533: bdg console --list 2>&1
534: 
535: **Validation**: `operations_complete`

537: # Cleanup happens automatically on exit (success or error)
538: # → Session always stopped
539: # → Resources always released

15: 
16: # Advanced Session Management
17: 
18: Advanced patterns for session lifecycle, multi-session handling, and state persistence.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: Always verify session state before operations - session failures cascade. Implement proper cleanup patterns (trap-based) to prevent resource leaks and orphaned browser processes.
25: 
26: ---
27: 
28: ## 2. PREREQUISITES
29: 
30: **Foundation:** Follow session basics from SKILL.md Section 3 before using advanced patterns:
31: - **Session Lifecycle**: Start → Verify → Execute → Stop workflow
32: - **Session States**: inactive, starting, active, error
33: - **Basic Verification**: `bdg status 2>&1 | jq '.state'`
34: - See [../SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) Section 3 "HOW IT WORKS"
35: 
36: **Recommended Tools**:
37: - `jq` for JSON parsing (install: `brew install jq` or `apt-get install jq`)
38: - Bash 4.0+ for array support and trap handling
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## 3. SESSION LIFECYCLE
43: 
44: ### Basic Lifecycle Pattern
45: 
46: ```bash
47: # 1. Start session
48: bdg <url>
49: 
50: # 2. Verify session active
51: bdg status
52: 
53: # 3. Execute operations
54: bdg cdp <Method>
55: bdg dom screenshot output.png
56: bdg console --list
57: 
58: # 4. Stop session
59: bdg stop
60: ```
61: 
62: **Session States**:
63: - `inactive` - No browser connection
64: - `starting` - Browser launching
65: - `active` - Ready for commands
66: - `error` - Connection failed
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 4. SESSION START PATTERNS
71: 
72: ### Standard Start
73: 
74: ```bash
75: # Start with URL
76: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
77: 
78: # Check if started successfully
79: if bdg status 2>&1 | grep -q "active"; then
80:   echo "Session ready"
81: else
82:   echo "Session failed to start"
83:   exit 1
84: fi
85: ```
86: 
87: ### Start with Retry Logic
88: 
89: ```bash
90: #!/bin/bash
91: # Robust session start with retries
92: 
93: MAX_RETRIES=3
94: RETRY_DELAY=2
95: 
96: start_session() {
97:   local url=$1
98:   local attempt=1
99: 
100:   while [ $attempt -le $MAX_RETRIES ]; do
101:     echo "Attempt $attempt: Starting session for $url"
102: 
103:     bdg "$url" 2>&1
104:     sleep $RETRY_DELAY
105: 
106:     if bdg status 2>&1 | grep -q "active"; then
107:       echo "Session started successfully"
108:       return 0
109:     fi
110: 
111:     echo "Retry $attempt failed"
112:     attempt=$((attempt + 1))
113:     sleep $((RETRY_DELAY * attempt))
114:   done
115: 
116:   echo "Failed to start session after $MAX_RETRIES attempts"
117:   return 1
118: }
119: 
120: start_session "https://example.com"
121: ```
122: 
123: ### Start with Timeout
124: 
125: ```bash
126: #!/bin/bash
127: # Session start with timeout
128: 
129: SESSION_TIMEOUT=30
130: 
131: start_with_timeout() {
132:   local url=$1
133: 
134:   # Start in background
135:   bdg "$url" 2>&1 &
136:   local pid=$!
137: 
138:   # Wait with timeout
139:   local elapsed=0
140:   while [ $elapsed -lt $SESSION_TIMEOUT ]; do
141:     if bdg status 2>&1 | grep -q "active"; then
142:       echo "Session active after ${elapsed}s"
143:       return 0
144:     fi
145:     sleep 1
146:     elapsed=$((elapsed + 1))
147:   done
148: 
149:   echo "Session timeout after ${SESSION_TIMEOUT}s"
150:   kill $pid 2>/dev/null
151:   return 1
152: }
153: 
154: start_with_timeout "https://example.com"
155: ```
156: 
157: ---
158: 
159: ## 5. SESSION STATUS VERIFICATION
160: 
161: ### Status Check Patterns
162: 
163: ```bash
164: # Simple status check
165: bdg status 2>&1
166: 
167: # Check and extract state
168: session_state=$(bdg status 2>&1 | jq -r '.state')
169: echo "Current state: $session_state"
170: 
171: # Conditional execution based on status
172: if bdg status 2>&1 | jq -e '.state == "active"' > /dev/null; then
173:   bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
174: else
175:   echo "Session not active, cannot capture screenshot"
176: fi
177: ```
178: 
179: ### Health Check Function
180: 
181: ```bash
182: #!/bin/bash
183: # Comprehensive session health check
184: 
185: check_session_health() {
186:   # Check if bdg is installed
187:   command -v bdg >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
188:     echo "ERROR: bdg not installed"
189:     echo "Install: npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha"
190:     return 1
191:   }
192: 
193:   # Check session status
194:   local status_output=$(bdg status 2>&1)
195:   local exit_code=$?
196: 
197:   if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
198:     echo "ERROR: Status check failed"
199:     echo "$status_output"
200:     return 1
201:   fi
202: 
203:   # Parse status
204:   local state=$(echo "$status_output" | jq -r '.state // "unknown"')
205: 
206:   case "$state" in
207:     active)
208:       echo "✓ Session healthy and active"
209:       return 0
210:       ;;
211:     starting)
212:       echo "⚠ Session starting..."
213:       return 2
214:       ;;
215:     inactive)
216:       echo "✗ No active session"
217:       return 3
218:       ;;
219:     error)
220:       echo "✗ Session in error state"
221:       echo "$status_output" | jq '.error // "Unknown error"'
222:       return 4
223:       ;;
224:     *)
225:       echo "✗ Unknown session state: $state"
226:       return 5
227:       ;;
228:   esac
229: }
230: 
231: check_session_health
232: ```
233: 
234: ---
235: 
236: ## 6. MULTI-SESSION MANAGEMENT
237: 
238: ### Sequential Session Labeling (No True Concurrency)
239: 
240: Live `bdg 0.6.10 --help` exposes one global `status` / `stop` lifecycle with no session-id, name, or selector option. A locally-tracked bash label does not select a specific bdg session: every `bdg status` / `bdg stop` call still targets the single active session, so two "tracked" sessions started back to back are not actually isolated from each other, and the second `bdg <url>` replaces the first. Label sessions for reporting only, and fully finish one (start, verify, use, stop) before starting the next. For true parallel browser control, use the `mcp-tooling/mcp-chrome-devtools` MCP surface's multiple registered instances (see `SKILL.md`) instead of the `bdg` CLI.
241: 
242: ```bash
243: #!/bin/bash
244: # Label sessions for reporting, but process them one at a time.
245: # bdg has exactly one active session; there is no selector to address a
246: # specific labeled session once it is running.
247: 
248: # Session tracking (label -> url, for reporting only)
249: declare -A SESSIONS
250: 
251: run_labeled_session() {
252:   local name=$1
253:   local url=$2
254: 
255:   echo "Starting session: $name"
256:   bdg "$url" 2>&1
257:   SESSIONS[$name]="$url"
258: 
259:   if bdg status 2>&1 | grep -q "active"; then
260:     echo "✓ Session $name active"
261:   else
262:     echo "✗ Session $name failed"
263:     unset SESSIONS[$name]
264:     return 1
265:   fi
266: 
267:   # ... do the work for this session here, before it is stopped ...
268: 
269:   echo "Stopping session: $name"
270:   bdg stop 2>&1
271:   unset SESSIONS[$name]
272: }
273: 
274: # Usage: fully start, use, and stop one session before starting the next
275: run_labeled_session "production" "https://example.com"
276: run_labeled_session "staging" "https://staging.example.com"
277: ```
278: 
279: ### Sequential Session Processing
280: 
281: ```bash
282: #!/bin/bash
283: # Process multiple URLs sequentially with session cleanup
284: 
285: urls=(
286:   "https://example.com"
287:   "https://test.com"
288:   "https://demo.com"
289: )
290: 
291: process_url() {
292:   local url=$1
293:   local filename=$(echo "$url" | sed 's|https://||' | sed 's|/|-|g')
294: 
295:   echo "Processing: $url"
296: 
297:   # Start session
298:   bdg "$url" 2>&1 || return 1
299: 
300:   # Wait for page load
301:   sleep 3
302: 
303:   # Capture data
304:   bdg dom screenshot "${filename}.png" 2>&1
305:   bdg console --list 2>&1 > "${filename}-console.json"
306:   bdg network har "${filename}.har" 2>&1
307: 
308:   # Cleanup
309:   bdg stop 2>&1
310: 
311:   echo "✓ Completed: $url"
312: }
313: 
314: # Process each URL
315: for url in "${urls[@]}"; do
316:   process_url "$url" || echo "Failed: $url"
317:   sleep 2  # Cool-down between sessions
318: done
319: ```
320: 
321: ---
322: 
323: ## 7. SESSION RESUMPTION
324: 
325: ### Resume Check Pattern
326: 
327: ```bash
328: #!/bin/bash
329: # Check if session can be resumed or needs restart
330: 
331: resume_or_start() {
332:   local url=$1
333: 
334:   # Check if session already active
335:   if bdg status 2>&1 | jq -e '.state == "active"' > /dev/null; then
336:     echo "Resuming existing session"
337: 
338:     # Verify session URL matches
339:     current_url=$(bdg cdp Page.getNavigationHistory 2>&1 | \
340:       jq -r '.result.entries[-1].url // ""')
341: 
342:     if [[ "$current_url" =~ ^"$url" ]]; then
343:       echo "✓ Session URL matches, resuming"
344:       return 0
345:     else
346:       echo "⚠ Session URL mismatch, restarting"
347:       bdg stop 2>&1
348:     fi
349:   fi
350: 
351:   # Start new session
352:   echo "Starting new session"
353:   bdg "$url" 2>&1
354: }
355: 
356: resume_or_start "https://example.com"
357: ```
358: 
359: ### Session State Persistence
360: 
361: ```bash
362: #!/bin/bash
363: # Save and restore session state
364: 
365: SESSION_STATE_FILE="/tmp/bdg-session-state.json"
366: 
367: save_session_state() {
368:   echo "Saving session state..."
369: 
370:   local state=$(bdg status 2>&1)
371:   local cookies=$(bdg network getCookies 2>&1)
372:   local url=$(bdg cdp Page.getNavigationHistory 2>&1 | \
373:     jq -r '.result.entries[-1].url')
374: 
375:   jq -n \
376:     --argjson status "$state" \
377:     --argjson cookies "$cookies" \
378:     --arg url "$url" \
379:     '{
380:       timestamp: now,
381:       url: $url,
382:       status: $status,
383:       cookies: $cookies
384:     }' > "$SESSION_STATE_FILE"
385: 
386:   echo "✓ Session state saved to $SESSION_STATE_FILE"
387: }
388: 
389: restore_session_state() {
390:   if [ ! -f "$SESSION_STATE_FILE" ]; then
391:     echo "No saved session state found"
392:     return 1
393:   fi
394: 
395:   echo "Restoring session state..."
396: 
397:   local url=$(jq -r '.url' "$SESSION_STATE_FILE")
398:   local cookies=$(jq -r '.cookies' "$SESSION_STATE_FILE")
399: 
400:   # Start session
401:   bdg "$url" 2>&1
402: 
403:   # Restore cookies
404:   echo "$cookies" | jq -r '.[] | @json' | while read cookie; do
405:     bdg cdp Network.setCookie "$cookie" 2>&1 > /dev/null
406:   done
407: 
408:   echo "✓ Session state restored"
409: }
410: 
411: # Usage
412: save_session_state
413: bdg stop 2>&1
414: restore_session_state
415: ```
416: 
417: ---
418: 
419: ## 8. ERROR HANDLING
420: 
421: ### Session Error Recovery
422: 
423: ```bash
424: #!/bin/bash
425: # Recover from session errors
426: 
427: recover_session() {
428:   local url=$1
429:   local max_attempts=3
430: 
431:   for attempt in $(seq 1 $max_attempts); do
432:     echo "Recovery attempt $attempt..."
433: 
434:     # Stop any existing session
435:     bdg stop 2>&1 2>/dev/null
436: 
437:     # Wait before retry
438:     sleep 2
439: 
440:     # Start new session
441:     bdg "$url" 2>&1
442: 
443:     # Verify
444:     if check_session_health; then
445:       echo "✓ Session recovered"
446:       return 0
447:     fi
448:   done
449: 
450:   echo "✗ Session recovery failed after $max_attempts attempts"
451:   return 1
452: }
453: 
454: # Usage
455: if ! check_session_health; then
456:   recover_session "https://example.com"
457: fi
458: ```
459: 
460: ### Graceful Degradation
461: 
462: ```bash
463: #!/bin/bash
464: # Fallback to alternative approaches on session failure
465: 
466: capture_with_fallback() {
467:   local url=$1
468:   local output=$2
469: 
470:   # Try bdg dom screenshot
471:   if bdg dom screenshot "$output" 2>&1; then
472:     echo "✓ Screenshot captured with bdg"
473:     return 0
474:   fi
475: 
476:   echo "⚠ bdg failed, trying CDP method..."
477: 
478:   # Fallback to CDP screenshot
479:   if bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1 | \
480:      jq -r '.result.data' | \
481:      base64 -d > "$output"; then
482:     echo "✓ Screenshot captured with CDP"
483:     return 0
484:   fi
485: 
486:   echo "✗ All screenshot methods failed"
487:   return 1
488: }
489: 
490: capture_with_fallback "https://example.com" "output.png"
491: ```
492: 
493: ---
494: 
495: ## 9. SESSION CLEANUP
496: 
497: ### Before/After: Cleanup Patterns
498: 
499: ❌ **BEFORE** (Anti-pattern - No cleanup):
500: ```bash
501: #!/bin/bash
502: # Missing cleanup - resource leak risk
503: 
504: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
505: bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
506: bdg console --list 2>&1
507: 
508: # Script exits without stopping session
509: # → Browser process remains running
510: # → Session resources not released
511: # → Next script may fail with "session already active"
512: ```
513: 
514: ✅ **AFTER** (Correct - Trap-based cleanup):
515: ```bash
516: #!/bin/bash
517: # Automatic cleanup via trap handler
518: 
519: cleanup() {
520:   echo "Cleaning up session..."
521:   bdg stop 2>&1 > /dev/null
522:   echo "✓ Cleanup complete"
523: }
524: 
525: # Register cleanup on EXIT, INT (Ctrl+C), TERM
526: trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM
527: 
528: **Validation**: `cleanup_registered`
529: 
530: # Session work
531: bdg https://example.com 2>&1
532: bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
533: bdg console --list 2>&1
534: 
535: **Validation**: `operations_complete`
536: 
537: # Cleanup happens automatically on exit (success or error)
538: # → Session always stopped
539: # → Resources always released
540: # → No orphaned processes
541: ```
542: 
543: **Why better**: Cleanup guaranteed even on errors/interrupts, prevents resource leaks, ensures deterministic state.
544: 
545: ### Cleanup Verification
546: 
547: ```bash
548: #!/bin/bash
549: # Verify session stopped successfully
550: 
551: stop_and_verify() {
552:   echo "Stopping session..."
553: 
554:   bdg stop 2>&1
555: 
556:   # Wait briefly
557:   sleep 1
558: 
559:   # Verify stopped
560:   if bdg status 2>&1 | jq -e '.state == "inactive"' > /dev/null; then
561:     echo "✓ Session stopped successfully"
562:     return 0
563:   else
564:     echo "⚠ Session may still be active"
565:     return 1
566:   fi
567: }
568: 
569: stop_and_verify
570: ```
571: 
572: ---
573: 
574: ## 10. PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION
575: 
576: ### Session Pooling Pattern
577: 
578: ```bash
579: #!/bin/bash
580: # Keep session warm for multiple operations
581: 
582: SESSION_WARMUP_URL="https://example.com"
583: SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT=60
584: 
585: warm_session() {
586:   # Check if session active
587:   if bdg status 2>&1 | jq -e '.state == "active"' > /dev/null; then
588:     echo "Session already warm"
589:     return 0
590:   fi
591: 
592:   # Start warmup session
593:   echo "Warming up session..."
594:   bdg "$SESSION_WARMUP_URL" 2>&1
595: 
596:   # Pre-enable common domains
597:   bdg cdp Network.enable 2>&1 > /dev/null
598:   bdg cdp Runtime.enable 2>&1 > /dev/null
599:   bdg cdp DOM.enable 2>&1 > /dev/null
600: 
601:   echo "✓ Session warmed up and ready"
602: }
603: 
604: # Keep session alive during idle
605: keep_alive() {
606:   local last_use=$(date +%s)
607: 
608:   while true; do
609:     local now=$(date +%s)
610:     local idle=$((now - last_use))
611: 
612:     if [ $idle -gt $SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT ]; then
613:       echo "Session idle timeout, stopping..."
614:       bdg stop 2>&1
615:       break
616:     fi
617: 
618:     sleep 10
619:   done
620: }
621: 
622: # Usage
623: warm_session
624: # ... perform operations ...
625: keep_alive &
626: ```
627: 
628: ### Batch Operations
629: 
630: ```bash
631: #!/bin/bash
632: # Batch multiple operations in single session
633: 
634: batch_operations() {
635:   local url=$1
636:   shift
637:   local operations=("$@")
638: 
639:   # Start session once
640:   bdg "$url" 2>&1
641: 
642:   # Execute all operations
643:   for op in "${operations[@]}"; do
644:     echo "Executing: $op"
645:     eval "$op" 2>&1
646:   done
647: 
648:   # Stop once
649:   bdg stop 2>&1
650: }
651: 
652: # Usage
653: batch_operations "https://example.com" \
654:   "bdg dom screenshot page.png" \
655:   "bdg console --list > console.json" \
656:   "bdg network getCookies > cookies.json" \
657:   "bdg network har network.har"
658: ```
659: 
660: ---
661: 
662: ## 11. BEST PRACTICES
663: 
664: 1. **Always verify session state** before executing operations
665: 2. **Use trap for cleanup** to ensure sessions are stopped on script exit
666: 3. **Implement retry logic** for production scripts
667: 4. **Track multiple sessions** with metadata when running concurrent operations
668: 5. **Save session state** for resumption after interruptions
669: 6. **Enable common domains upfront** (Network, Runtime, DOM) for better performance
670: 7. **Implement health checks** with meaningful error messages
671: 8. **Use timeouts** to prevent hanging on failed session starts
672: 9. **Clean up sessions** promptly to release browser resources
673: 10. **Log session lifecycle events** for debugging

54: # 3. Check session status
55: bdg status 2>&1
56: 
57: # 4. Check Chrome/Chromium availability
58: which google-chrome chromium-browser chromium 2>/dev/null
59: 
60: # 5. Check node/npm versions
61: node --version
62: npm --version
63: ```
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 4. INSTALLATION ISSUES
68: 
69: ### Issue: bdg command not found
70: 
71: **Symptoms**:
72: ```bash
73: $ bdg https://example.com
74: bash: bdg: command not found
75: ```
76: 
77: **Diagnosis**:
78: ```bash
79: # Check if installed
80: npm list -g browser-debugger-cli
81: 
82: # Check npm global bin path
83: npm config get prefix
84: echo $PATH
85: ```
86: 
87: **Solutions**:
88: 
89: 1. **Install bdg**:
90:    ```bash
91:    npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha
92:    ```
93: 
94: 2. **Fix PATH if npm bin not in PATH**:
95:    ```bash
96:    # Find npm global bin directory
97:    NPM_BIN=$(npm config get prefix)/bin
98: 
99:    # Add to PATH (bash)
100:    echo 'export PATH="$PATH:'$NPM_BIN'"' >> ~/.bashrc
101:    source ~/.bashrc
102: 
103:    # Add to PATH (zsh)
104:    echo 'export PATH="$PATH:'$NPM_BIN'"' >> ~/.zshrc
105:    source ~/.zshrc
106:    ```
107: 
108: 3. **Use npx as alternative**:
109:    ```bash
110:    npx browser-debugger-cli https://example.com
111:    ```
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ### Issue: npm install fails
116: 
117: **Symptoms**:
118: ```bash
119: $ npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha
120: npm ERR! code EACCES
121: npm ERR! syscall access
122: ```
123: 
124: **Diagnosis**:
125: ```bash
126: # Check npm permissions
127: npm config get prefix
128: ls -la $(npm config get prefix)
129: ```
130: 
131: **Solutions**:
132: 
133: 1. **Use npx (no global install needed)**:
134:    ```bash
135:    npx browser-debugger-cli@alpha https://example.com
136:    ```
137: 
138: 2. **Fix npm permissions** (recommended):
139:    ```bash
140:    mkdir ~/.npm-global
141:    npm config set prefix '~/.npm-global'
142:    echo 'export PATH=~/.npm-global/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
143:    source ~/.bashrc
144: 
145:    npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha
146:    ```
147: 
148: 3. **Use sudo** (not recommended):
149:    ```bash
150:    sudo npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha
151:    ```
152: 
153: ---
154: 
155: ### Issue: Wrong Node version
156: 
157: **Symptoms**:
158: ```bash
159: $ bdg --version
160: Error: Node version too old
161: ```
162: 
163: **Diagnosis**:
164: ```bash
165: node --version
166: # bdg requires Node.js 14.x or higher
167: ```
168: 
169: **Solution**:
170: ```bash
171: # Install/update Node.js
172: # Using nvm (recommended)
173: curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.0/install.sh | bash
174: nvm install 18
175: nvm use 18
176: 
177: # Or download from nodejs.org
178: ```
179: 
180: ---
181: 
182: ## 5. BROWSER CONNECTION ISSUES
183: 
184: ### Issue: Browser not found
185: 
186: **Symptoms**:
187: ```bash
188: $ bdg https://example.com
189: Error: Could not find Chrome/Chromium executable
190: ```
191: 
192: **Diagnosis**:
193: ```bash
194: # Check for Chrome/Chromium
195: which google-chrome google-chrome-stable chromium chromium-browser
196: 
197: # Check environment variable
198: echo $CHROME_PATH
199: ```
200: 
201: **Solutions**:
202: 
203: 1. **macOS**:
204:    ```bash
205:    # Set Chrome path
206:    export CHROME_PATH="/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome"
207: 
208:    # Add to shell profile
209:    echo 'export CHROME_PATH="/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome"' >> ~/.zshrc
210:    ```
211: 
212: 2. **Linux**:
213:    ```bash
214:    # Install Chromium
215:    sudo apt-get install chromium-browser  # Debian/Ubuntu
216:    sudo yum install chromium              # RHEL/CentOS
217:    sudo pacman -S chromium                # Arch
218: 
219:    # Or set custom path
220:    export CHROME_PATH=/usr/bin/chromium-browser
221:    ```
222: 
223: 3. **Windows (WSL)**:
224:    ```bash
225:    # Install Chrome in WSL or point to Windows Chrome
226:    export CHROME_PATH="/mnt/c/Program Files/Google/Chrome/Application/chrome.exe"
227:    ```
228: 
229: ---
230: 
231: ### Before/After: Systematic Troubleshooting
232: 
233: ❌ **BEFORE** (Anti-pattern - Guessing fixes):
234: ```bash
235: # Browser won't launch - trying random fixes
236: export CHROME_PATH=/usr/bin/chrome  # Guess 1
237: bdg https://example.com 2>&1  # Still fails
238: 
239: killall chrome  # Guess 2
240: bdg https://example.com 2>&1  # Still fails
241: 
242: sudo bdg https://example.com 2>&1  # Guess 3 - dangerous!
243: # Still fails, now with permission issues
244: 
245: # Results: Wasted time, created new problems, no root cause identified
246: ```
247: 
248: ✅ **AFTER** (Correct - Systematic diagnosis):
249: ```bash
250: # Step 1: Run 5-check diagnostic sequence
251: command -v bdg  # → ✓ Installed
252: 
253: **Validation**: `installation_verified`
254: 
255: bdg --version 2>&1  # → ✓ v1.0.0
256: 
257: **Validation**: `version_confirmed`
258: 
259: which google-chrome chromium-browser  # → ✗ Not found
260: 
261: **Validation**: `browser_missing` (root cause identified!)
262: 
263: # Step 2: Fix root cause (install browser)
264: brew install --cask google-chrome  # macOS
265: 
266: **Validation**: `browser_installed`
267: 
268: # Step 3: Verify fix
269: bdg https://example.com 2>&1  # → ✓ Works!
270: 
271: **Validation**: `session_started`
272: ```
273: 
274: **Why better**: Systematic approach finds root cause, no guessing, verifiable checkpoints, prevents cascading issues.
275: 
276: ---
277: 
278: ### Issue: Browser launch fails
279: 
280: **Symptoms**:
281: ```bash
282: $ bdg https://example.com
283: Error: Failed to launch browser
284: Timeout waiting for browser connection
285: ```
286: 
287: **Diagnosis**:
288: ```bash
289: # Check if Chrome can launch manually
290: google-chrome --version
291: 
292: # Check for conflicting processes
293: ps aux | grep chrome
294: 
295: # Check available ports
296: netstat -an | grep 9222  # Default debugging port
297: ```
298: 
299: **Solutions**:
300: 
301: 1. **Kill existing Chrome instances**:
302:    ```bash
303:    # macOS/Linux
304:    pkill -f chrome
305: 
306:    # Verify
307:    ps aux | grep chrome
308:    ```
309: 
310: 2. **Use different debugging port**:
311:    ```bash
312:    export CHROME_DEBUGGING_PORT=9223
313:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
314:    ```
315: 
316: 3. **Run with headless mode** (if display issues):
317:    ```bash
318:    export CHROME_HEADLESS=true
319:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
320:    ```
321: 
322: 4. **Check permissions** (Linux):
323:    ```bash
324:    # Add to chrome-sandbox group
325:    sudo chown root:root /opt/google/chrome/chrome-sandbox
326:    sudo chmod 4755 /opt/google/chrome/chrome-sandbox
327:    ```
328: 
329: ---
330: 
331: ## 6. SESSION MANAGEMENT ISSUES
332: 
333: ### Issue: Session won't start
334: 
335: **Symptoms**:
336: ```bash
337: $ bdg https://example.com
338: $ bdg status
339: { "state": "inactive" }
340: ```
341: 
342: **Diagnosis**:
343: ```bash
344: # Check stderr output
345: bdg https://example.com 2>&1 | tee debug.log
346: 
347: # Check system resources
348: free -h  # Linux
349: vm_stat  # macOS
350: 
351: # Check network connectivity
352: curl -I https://example.com
353: ```
354: 
355: **Solutions**:
356: 
357: 1. **Verify URL is accessible**:
358:    ```bash
359:    curl -I https://example.com
360:    # Should return HTTP 200 OK
361:    ```
362: 
363: 2. **Increase timeout**:
364:    ```bash
365:    export BDG_TIMEOUT=60000  # 60 seconds
366:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
367:    ```
368: 
369: 3. **Check for certificate errors**:
370:    ```bash
371:    # Bypass SSL verification (not for production)
372:    export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
373:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
374:    ```
375: 
376: 4. **Start with simpler URL**:
377:    ```bash
378:    # Test with simple page first
379:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
380:    ```
381: 
382: ---
383: 
384: ### Issue: Session stuck in "starting" state
385: 
386: **Symptoms**:
387: ```bash
388: $ bdg status
389: { "state": "starting", "duration": "300s" }
390: ```
391: 
392: **Diagnosis**:
393: ```bash
394: # Check Chrome process
395: ps aux | grep chrome
396: 
397: # Check logs
398: bdg status 2>&1 | jq '.logs // []'
399: ```
400: 
401: **Solutions**:
402: 
403: 1. **Force stop and restart**:
404:    ```bash
405:    bdg stop 2>&1
406:    sleep 3
407:    pkill -9 -f chrome  # Force kill if needed
408:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
409:    ```
410: 
411: 2. **Clear bdg state**:
412:    ```bash
413:    # Find and remove state files
414:    rm -rf ~/.bdg/state 2>/dev/null
415:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
416:    ```
417: 
418: ---
419: 
420: ### Issue: Multiple sessions conflict
421: 
422: **Symptoms**:
423: ```bash
424: $ bdg https://example.com
425: Error: Another session already active
426: ```
427: 
428: **Diagnosis**:
429: ```bash
430: bdg status 2>&1
431: ps aux | grep bdg
432: ```
433: 
434: **Solutions**:
435: 
436: 1. **Stop existing session**:
437:    ```bash
438:    bdg stop 2>&1
439:    ```
440: 
441: 2. **Kill all bdg processes**:
442:    ```bash
443:    pkill -f "bdg "
444:    pkill -f browser-debugger-cli
445:    ```
446: 
447: 3. **Use session management pattern**:
448:    ```bash
449:    # Check before starting
450:    if bdg status 2>&1 | jq -e '.state == "active"' > /dev/null; then
451:      echo "Stopping existing session"
452:      bdg stop 2>&1
453:    fi
454: 
455:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
456:    ```
457: 
458: ---
459: 
460: ## 7. CDP COMMAND ISSUES
461: 
462: ### Issue: CDP method not found
463: 
464: **Symptoms**:
465: ```bash
466: $ bdg cdp Page.screenshot
467: Error: Method not found: Page.screenshot
468: ```
469: 
470: **Diagnosis**:
471: ```bash
472: # Discover correct method name
473: bdg cdp --search screenshot
474: 
475: # Check domain
476: bdg cdp --describe Page
477: ```
478: 
479: **Solution**:
480: 
481: Use correct method name (case matters):
482: ```bash
483: # Correct
484: bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1
485: 
486: # Also works (bdg normalizes case)
487: bdg cdp page.capturescreenshot 2>&1
488: 
489: # Use helper instead
490: bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
491: ```
492: 
493: ---
494: 
495: ### Issue: CDP method fails with parameter error
496: 
497: **Symptoms**:
498: ```bash
499: $ bdg cdp Page.navigate '{"url":"example.com"}'
500: Error: Invalid URL format
501: ```
502: 
503: **Diagnosis**:
504: ```bash
505: # Check method signature
506: bdg cdp --describe Page.navigate
507: 
508: # Validate JSON
509: echo '{"url":"example.com"}' | jq .
510: ```
511: 
512: **Solutions**:
513: 
514: 1. **Fix parameter format**:
515:    ```bash
516:    # Use full URL with protocol
517:    bdg cdp Page.navigate '{"url":"https://example.com"}' 2>&1
518:    ```
519: 
520: 2. **Escape quotes properly**:
521:    ```bash
522:    # Use single quotes for JSON, double quotes inside
523:    bdg cdp Page.navigate '{"url":"https://example.com","referrer":"https://google.com"}' 2>&1
524: 
525:    # Or escape double quotes
526:    bdg cdp Page.navigate "{\"url\":\"https://example.com\"}" 2>&1
527:    ```
528: 
529: 3. **Use jq to build JSON**:
530:    ```bash
531:    params=$(jq -n --arg url "https://example.com" '{url: $url}')
532:    bdg cdp Page.navigate "$params" 2>&1
533:    ```
534: 
535: ---
536: 
537: ### Issue: Session required for CDP command
538: 
539: **Symptoms**:
540: ```bash
541: $ bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot
542: Error: No active session
543: ```
544: 
545: **Solution**:
546: 
547: Start session first:
548: ```bash
549: # Always verify session before CDP commands
550: if ! bdg status 2>&1 | jq -e '.state == "active"' > /dev/null; then
551:   bdg https://example.com 2>&1
552: fi
553: 
554: # Now execute CDP command
555: bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1
556: ```
557: 
558: ---
559: 
560: ## 8. OUTPUT PARSING ISSUES
561: 
562: ### Issue: jq parse error
563: 
564: **Symptoms**:
565: ```bash
566: $ bdg status | jq .
567: parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 10
568: ```
569: 
570: **Diagnosis**:
571: ```bash
572: # Check raw output
573: bdg status 2>&1
574: 
575: # Check if stderr mixed with stdout
576: bdg status 2>&1 | head
577: ```
578: 
579: **Solutions**:
580: 
581: 1. **Always use 2>&1 to capture stderr**:
582:    ```bash
583:    bdg status 2>&1 | jq '.'
584:    ```
585: 
586: 2. **Filter non-JSON lines**:
587:    ```bash
588:    bdg status 2>&1 | grep '^{' | jq '.'
589:    ```
590: 
591: 3. **Handle errors gracefully**:
592:    ```bash
593:    output=$(bdg status 2>&1)
594:    if echo "$output" | jq . > /dev/null 2>&1; then
595:      echo "$output" | jq '.state'
596:    else
597:      echo "Error: Invalid JSON output"
598:      echo "$output"
599:    fi
600:    ```
601: 
602: ---
603: 
604: ### Issue: Binary data in stdout
605: 
606: **Symptoms**:
607: ```bash
608: $ bdg dom screenshot - | jq .
609: Binary file (standard input) matches
610: ```
611: 
612: **Solution**:
613: 
614: Handle binary output correctly:
615: ```bash
616: # Save to file
617: bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
618: 
619: # Or pipe to base64
620: bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1 | jq -r '.result.data' | base64 -d > output.png
621: 
622: # Don't pipe binary to jq
623: ```
624: 
625: ---
626: 
627: ## 9. PERFORMANCE ISSUES
628: 
629: ### Issue: Slow CDP command execution
630: 
631: **Symptoms**:
632: ```bash
633: $ time bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot
634: real    0m15.432s  # Should be much faster
635: ```
636: 
637: **Diagnosis**:
638: ```bash
639: # Check network latency
640: ping example.com
641: 
642: # Check browser resources
643: bdg cdp Memory.getDOMCounters 2>&1
644: 
645: # Check page complexity
646: bdg dom eval "document.querySelectorAll('*').length" 2>&1
647: ```
648: 
649: **Solutions**:
650: 
651: 1. **Enable CDP domains once upfront**:
652:    ```bash
653:    # Enable at session start
654:    bdg https://example.com 2>&1
655:    bdg cdp Network.enable 2>&1
656:    bdg cdp Runtime.enable 2>&1
657:    bdg cdp DOM.enable 2>&1
658: 
659:    # Now commands execute faster
660:    bdg console --list 2>&1
661:    ```
662: 
663: 2. **Use helpers instead of raw CDP**:
664:    ```bash
665:     # Faster
666:     bdg dom screenshot output.png 2>&1
667: 
668:     # Slower (raw CDP)
669:    bdg cdp Page.captureScreenshot 2>&1 | jq -r '.result.data' | base64 -d > output.png
670:    ```
671: 
672: 3. **Reduce page complexity**:
673:    ```bash
674:    # Block images/media
675:    bdg cdp Network.setBlockedURLs '{"urls":["*.jpg","*.png","*.mp4"]}' 2>&1
676:    ```
677: 
678: ---
679: 
680: ### Issue: High memory usage
681: 
682: **Symptoms**:
683: ```bash
684: $ ps aux | grep chrome
685: ... 4.5G ...  # High memory
686: ```
687: 
688: **Solutions**:
689: 
690: 1. **Stop sessions promptly**:
691:    ```bash
692:    # Always cleanup
693:    trap "bdg stop 2>&1" EXIT
694:    ```
695: 
696: 2. **Limit concurrent sessions**:
697:    ```bash
698:    # Process sequentially instead of parallel
699:    for url in "${urls[@]}"; do
700:      bdg "$url" 2>&1
701:      # ... operations ...
702:      bdg stop 2>&1
703:    done
704:    ```
705: 
706: 3. **Clear cache between sessions**:
707:    ```bash
708:    bdg cdp Network.clearBrowserCache 2>&1
709:    bdg cdp Network.clearBrowserCookies 2>&1
710:    ```
711: 
712: ---
713: 
714: ## 10. PLATFORM-SPECIFIC ISSUES
715: 
716: ### macOS: Gatekeeper blocking Chrome
717: 
718: **Symptoms**:
719: ```bash
720: Error: Chrome blocked by Gatekeeper
721: ```
722: 
723: **Solution**:
724: ```bash
725: # Allow Chrome in Security & Privacy settings
726: # Or use command
727: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Google Chrome.app"
728: ```
729: 
730: ---
731: 
732: ### Linux: Sandbox issues
733: 
734: **Symptoms**:
735: ```bash
736: Error: Failed to move to new namespace
737: ```
738: 
739: **Solution**:
740: ```bash
741: # Disable sandbox (NOT for production)
742: export CHROME_DEVEL_SANDBOX=/dev/null
743: 
744: # Or fix permissions
745: sudo sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1
746: ```
747: 
748: ---
749: 
750: ### Windows (WSL): Display issues
751: 
752: **Symptoms**:
753: ```bash
754: Error: Could not open display
755: ```
756: 
757: **Solution**:
758: ```bash
759: # Use headless mode
760: export CHROME_HEADLESS=true
761: 
762: # Or setup X11 forwarding
763: export DISPLAY=:0
764: ```
765: 
766: ---
767: 
768: ## 11. ERROR CODE REFERENCE
769: 
770: | Exit Code | Meaning | Solution |
771: |-----------|---------|----------|
772: | 0 | Success | N/A |
773: | 1 | General error | Check stderr output |
774: | 2 | Installation issue | Verify bdg installed |
775: | 3 | Browser launch failed | Check Chrome/Chromium path |
776: | 4 | Session timeout | Increase timeout or check URL |
777: | 5 | CDP method error | Verify method name and parameters |
778: | 6 | No active session | Start session first |
779: | 127 | Command not found | Install bdg or fix PATH |
780: 
781: ---
782: 
783: ## 12. DEBUG MODE
784: 
785: **Enable verbose logging**:
786: ```bash
787: # Set debug environment variable
788: export DEBUG=bdg:*
789: 
790: # Run command
791: bdg https://example.com 2>&1 | tee debug.log
792: 
793: # Or increase log level
794: export BDG_LOG_LEVEL=debug
795: bdg status 2>&1
796: ```
797: 
798: ---
799: 
800: ## 13. GETTING HELP
801: 
802: 1. **Check documentation**: https://github.com/szymdzum/browser-debugger-cli
803: 2. **Search issues**: https://github.com/szymdzum/browser-debugger-cli/issues
804: 3. **Report bug** with:
805:    - bdg version (`bdg --version`)
806:    - Platform (macOS/Linux/WSL)
807:    - Node version (`node --version`)
808:    - Full error output (with `2>&1`)
809:    - Minimal reproduction steps
810: 
811: ---
812: 
813: ## 14. COMMON SOLUTIONS CHECKLIST
814: 
815: Before reporting issues, try these:
816: 
817: - [ ] bdg installed globally (`npm install -g browser-debugger-cli@alpha`)
818: - [ ] bdg in PATH (`command -v bdg`)
819: - [ ] Chrome/Chromium installed and accessible
820: - [ ] Session started before CDP commands
821: - [ ] Session stopped after operations
822: - [ ] Using `2>&1` to capture full output
823: - [ ] Valid JSON for CDP parameters
824: - [ ] Correct CDP method names (check with `--describe`)
825: - [ ] No conflicting Chrome processes
826: - [ ] Sufficient system resources (memory, CPU)
827: 
828: ---
829: 
830: ## 15. RELATED RESOURCES
831: 
832: ### Reference Files
833: - [session-management.md](./session-management.md) - Session lifecycle patterns for robust automation
834: - [cdp-patterns.md](./cdp-patterns.md) - CDP command examples and domain-specific patterns
835: 
836: ### Related Skills
837: - `mcp-chrome-devtools` - Main skill orchestrator for bdg CLI workflows
838:
